_comment: THE per-lesson hardware table. This file is the single source of truth: Terraform reads it
with jsondecode(), and infra/lib.sh reads it with jq. JSON rather than .tfvars precisely so
both can read the same bytes — a generated second copy is how the two drift apart.
kind is 'vm' (a Scaleway VM, console: Compute -> CPU & GPU Instances) or 'baremetal'
(Scaleway Elastic Metal, console: Bare Metal -> Elastic Metal). It is a per-lesson decision.
Lessons 1-5 all run on VMs, and that is a MEASURED choice rather than a cost optimisation.
Measured 2026-08-06 on this account, running the repo's own substrates and lessons unmodified:
* lesson 1's full scorecard is row-for-row identical on a VM and on EM-A116X-SSD metal
(all 17 findings, same BLOCKED/REACHED); rootless podman reports Rootless:true; runsc
reports 4.19.0-gvisor; the distro hardening the lessons lean on is the same
(unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2, perf_event_paranoid=4, kptr_restrict=1).
* a VM exposes /dev/kvm AND /dev/vhost-vsock (AMD EPYC 7543, svm, kvm_amd.nested=1), so
Kata boots a real guest — kernel 6.18.35, the same guest kernel the metal box recorded,
and lesson 4's surprise reproduces (guest unprivileged_bpf_disabled=0 vs node 2).
* lesson 5's NAT guest boots on a VM and takes a private primary address on its
default-route interface (192.168.122.0/24) — which is the whole point of that topology.
The older 'the guest must be L1, so lesson 5 needs metal' note was wrong: that symptom
(grub loads, kernel resets forever) was later traced to BIOS-vs-UEFI and seen on metal
too, which is why 50-nat-vm.sh passes --boot uefi.
What VMs buy, in order of how much it matters: Elastic Metal has a default quota of 2 on a
new organization, so four metal lessons could not be up at once and the reader had to run
them in batches; metal stock is per-offer and moves; and a metal OS install takes 10-15
minutes per box against under a minute for a VM. The money is a rounding error either way.
root_volume_gb is NOT a default worth trusting: a Scaleway VM's default root volume is 8 GB
usable and the Kata stack (nerdctl-full + kata-static) needs 9.3 GB. Metal's large local SSD
hid that, and the failure is a tar dying with 'No space left on device' mid-install.
Chapter 3 (lessons 6-9) shares ONE cluster, `chapter-03-k8s`, carrying all four of its
substrates at once. The four lessons carry `box` instead of hardware, and `box` is the ONLY
indirection in this file: lib.sh's lesson_box() resolves it, everything else keeps reading the
row it lands on. The point is not money — four small short-lived boxes cost about what one
bigger one does. It is that chapter 3's claim is `four boundaries, one cluster, one field
selects between them`, and on a box carrying only gVisor the `runtimeClassName: gvisor` in
lesson 7 is a choice from a menu of one. On the shared cluster the other three runtimes are
installed and provably working beside it, so the field is doing what the chapter says it does.
check.sh proves that at provision time: it dispatches per substrate, so a four-substrate entry
fires all four boundary assertions against the one node before any lesson runs.
The honest cost: running ONE chapter-3 lesson now installs all four substrates (~30 min rather
than ~8), because the menu is the point. infra/chapter-03.sh amortizes it over all
four and still destroys the box on an EXIT trap, so no teardown becomes a human's to remember.
Chapter 3 runs single-node k3s ON a disposable VM rather than against a
managed cluster (Scaleway Kapsule) or a nested one (minikube, kind). Three reasons, in order of
how much they matter:
* every boundary in the chapter is installed AT NODE LEVEL — runsc's binaries and a containerd
runtime, kata-static plus /dev/kvm, the OpenShell gateway. Managed node pools reconcile that
away, and minikube's docker driver nests the node inside a container, which breaks Kata and
makes lesson 6's 'the pod runs on the node's kernel' claim untrue of the thing you ran.
* a managed cluster hands you a kubeconfig, and a kubeconfig is a CREDENTIAL. k3s writes its
own on the box and it never leaves, so nothing has to be kept out of the repo by hand.
* k3s costs ~1.2 GB idle and 30-60 seconds, against 4-6 minutes to create a Kapsule cluster
whose nodes are billed at these very same VM prices. There is no money in it, only delay.
k3s enforces NetworkPolicy through an embedded kube-router controller (flannel alone does not),
which lesson 6 depends on — and which 60-k8s.sh ASSERTS rather than assumes, because a CNI that
accepts a NetworkPolicy object and silently ignores it is this repo's characteristic failure.
Prices are read live from the Scaleway catalogue by lib.sh — never hardcoded here, because a
stale price in a cost warning is worse than no price.

lesson-01-no-sandbox.why: The bare box IS the lesson. No engine, no runtime — the rogue agent runs as an ordinary host process, which is only acceptable on a machine that is destroyed minutes later.

lesson-02-container.why: Rootless podman on the VM's own kernel. The unprivileged `agent` user is created by cloud-init and is load-bearing: rootless is the claim this lesson makes, and a Scaleway VM otherwise logs in as root.

lesson-03-container-gvisor.why: runsc is user-space and needs no hardware feature. Registered as an opt-in podman runtime so the default stays crun and Part 3 can re-run the previous rung on the same box.

lesson-04-container-kata.why: Needs /dev/kvm and /dev/vhost-vsock, which this VM type has. PLAY2-MICRO (8 GB RAM) so the 2 GB guest and the containerd/buildkit stack coexist. 60 GB (up from 40) because the Kata stack measured 9.3 GB and 35-containerd-devmapper adds a 20 GB thin-pool data file plus 2 GB of metadata beside it: the files are SPARSE and thin-provisioned, so that is a ceiling rather than disk actually spent, but the volume has to be able to honour it. The 8 GB default root volume fails mid-tar long before any of that. 35 runs AFTER 30 and gives this box a SECOND hypervisor under Kata (Firecracker), which needs the devmapper snapshotter because Firecracker has virtio-block and no virtio-fs — the container rootfs has to arrive as a block device. Read from inside, that is the whole difference: rootfs=virtiofs under kata-qemu, rootfs=ext4 under kata-fc.

lesson-05-container-openshell.why: OpenShell's rootless-podman driver refuses to start when the host's default-route address is public, and every Scaleway box has one. 50-nat-vm builds a libvirt guest on virbr0 whose primary address is private; the lesson then runs INSIDE that guest, reached through this box. Needs /dev/kvm for the guest and disk for its image.

chapter-03-k8s.why: NOT a lesson — the k3s cluster lessons 6, 7 and 8 share. It carries the four boundaries a workload selects with `runtimeClassName` (none / gvisor / kata-qemu / kata-fc) so that field is a real choice from a menu rather than the only runtime installed: measured 2026-08-13, one node served kernel 6.8.0-106-generic to a plain pod, 4.19.0-gvisor to a gVisor pod and guest 6.18.35 to a Kata pod, and installing Kata did NOT make it the default. 75 adds the devmapper snapshotter, which is what makes `kata-fc` — a class kata-deploy has always registered here and which has never worked — actually run: Firecracker has virtio-block and no virtio-fs, so a container rootfs must arrive as a BLOCK device, and without the snapshotter a kata-fc pod dies at sandbox creation with `snapshotter must be provided to unpack`. It configures no per-runtime snapshotter and must not: kata-deploy already writes `snapshotter = "devmapper"` on kata-fc and on nothing else, so kata-qemu stays on overlayfs and the split comes free and correct from upstream. ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING and it is about restarts, not files: 70 and 75 both run `systemctl restart k3s`, and nothing may restart k3s after 80, because a restart terminates the kata-deploy DaemonSet pod and that pod reverts its own install on termination. 75 sits between them for exactly that reason — loading a snapshotter needs containerd restarted, k3s embeds containerd, and there is no post-80 seam to do it in. 80 GB (up from 60) for 75's 25 GB thin-pool data file plus 2 GB of metadata; both are SPARSE and thin-provisioned, so that is a ceiling rather than disk spent. WHY LESSON 9 IS NOT HERE, and it is a capacity limit rather than a design one: with 90-k8s-openshell also installed, the OpenShell gateway and agent-sandbox controller stay RESIDENT from provisioning onward, and lesson 8's Part 3b — which boots Kata guests repeatedly to time the VM tax — took the whole box down (ssh dropped mid-run, lesson 9 could not reach it at all). Lesson 8 had passed that same Part 3b on an 8 GB box carrying 60+80 and no gateway, which is what points at memory. The obvious fix is a bigger box and it is NOT AVAILABLE on this account: POP2-4C-16G, PRO2-XS, BASIC3-X4C-16G and BASIC3-X6C-24G every one report `has reached its quota (0/0)`, PLAY2-MICRO is the largest PLAY2, and this CLI has no `scw account quota` subcommand to check before paying for a failed create. If that quota is ever raised, adding `chapter-3/90-k8s-openshell` back to this list and giving lesson-09 a `box` is a two-line change. 60 GB (up from lesson 8's 40) because Kata's 9.3 GB now shares the disk with gVisor's runsc and the agent image.

lesson-06-k8s.why: Runs on the shared cluster. The plain Pod rung: no runtimeClassName at all, which on a cluster where gvisor and kata-qemu are both registered is a deliberate abstention rather than an absence — kata-deploy does not make Kata the default, so 'the pod runs on the NODE kernel' stays literally true of the thing you ran, and check.sh asserts exactly that before any lesson starts.

lesson-07-k8s-gvisor.why: Runs on the shared cluster. `runtimeClassName: gvisor` selected from a menu that also holds kata-qemu — which is the whole reason the field exists and the reason this lesson stopped being a box with one runtime on it.

lesson-08-k8s-kata.why: Runs on the shared cluster. Reads the RuntimeClass list rather than hardcoding a name (kata-deploy registers ~25 and the set moves between releases), then picks kata-qemu — a selection that is only meaningful because gvisor is sitting in the same list.

lesson-09-k8s-openshell.why: The ONE chapter-3 lesson that keeps its own box, and the reason is capacity, not principle — see chapter-03-k8s's `why`. The Agent Sandbox controller, the OpenShell gateway StatefulSet and its PVC all land on this node alongside k3s; the prior art measured that path at roughly 4 CPU / 8 GB, so with Kata's repeated guest boots on the same machine the box died. It also loses the least by being separate: OpenShell is the one chapter-3 boundary NOT selected with `runtimeClassName` — its sandbox pods take their runtime class from the GATEWAY, because `openshell sandbox create` has no such flag — so it was never part of the per-pod runtime menu the shared cluster exists to demonstrate. Note what is NOT here: lesson 5's 50-nat-vm. The public-default-route constraint belongs to OpenShell's rootless-podman driver, and the kubernetes driver's sandbox callback is an in-cluster Service on a private ClusterIP.

openshift-sno.why: NOT a lesson — it is the single-node OpenShift CLUSTER that chapter 4's four lessons (10-13) all share. One entry rather than four, because installing SNO takes far longer than a lesson does and re-installing it four times would be absurd. It lives in this table so Terraform owns it and `down.sh --all` sweeps it: at EUR 0.263/hr, forgetting this box is the single most expensive mistake available in this repo. Metal is genuinely required here (Kata needs /dev/kvm AND cluster-admin on a real node); it is the ONLY place in the tutorial that is true. `substrates` is empty on purpose: the SNO install cannot run through up.sh's substrate model, because it REPLACES the operating system mid-flight — the box that finishes the install is RHCOS and has no `agent` user, no repo checkout and no uv. It is driven instead by infra/openshift-sno/install.sh, which runs on the workstation.
